reading_plan: Source title: Making AI Less 'Thirsty': Uncovering and addressing the secret water footprint of AI models. Source type: other. First look: an eight-page Communications of the ACM sustainability feature (printed pp. 54–61), with a full-page conceptual illustration, a cooling-system diagram, a dense numerical table, a three-panel figure, inline equations, and a 33-entry reference list. The writing alternates accessible explanatory and advocacy prose with technical accounting and assumption-heavy estimates. I will follow the article in order at natural paragraph and subsection boundaries, usually roughly 200–500 source words per step, taking shorter steps where definitions, equations, the numerical table, or qualifications require closer attention. Page-top visual elements and continuous cross-page paragraphs are read together with their local discussion; figure, table, and equation readings are paraphrases. The reading records the authors’ claims and support without testing their ultimate validity or importing a research question.

Water consumption is withdrawal minus discharge and covers water evaporated, transpired, incorporated into products or crops, or otherwise removed from the immediate water environment.

reading_path.location: p. 57 (PDF p. 4), How does AI use water? and Scope-1 water usage through facility-level cooling
reading_path.moves: Classifies water use into scopes and explains the physical chain from server heat to facility heat rejection. Distinguishes liquid circulation from evaporation.

claims.text: AI uses onsite water for datacenter cooling (scope 1), offsite water for electricity generation (scope 2), and supply-chain water for server manufacturing (scope 3).
Nearly all server energy becomes heat that must be removed to avoid overheating, through server-level cooling followed by facility-level cooling.

Server-level air or liquid cooling transfers heat to facility air or a heat exchanger without evaporating or consuming water; newer AI-training datacenters often use liquid cooling because server power densities are high.
Facility-level cooling rejects heat outdoors; cooling towers and water-evaporation-assisted air cooling are two common water-intensive approaches.
